confirmed.statement: The document states random assignment. Section 3.2.1 says 'participants were randomly assigned to one condition for the first task and then switched to the other condition for the second task', which is the form's quote, verbatim. The abstract, the Introduction, and Section 4.1 ('the random assignment did not introduce bias') repeat it.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.1; p. 1, Abstract; p. 2, Introduction; p. 8, Section 4.1

confirmed.statement: People were randomized one by one, not as intact classes. All students met in one lecture hall and 'were then randomly divided into two groups'. Fig. 1 gives Group A 24 students (unaided first) and Group B 27 students (ChatGPT first). The groups did not differ on five prior assignments or GPA (all p > .24).
confirmed.locator: pp. 4-5, Section 3.2.1; p. 5, Fig. 1; p. 7, Table 3; p. 9, Table 5 note

confirmed.statement: The order of conditions was randomized, as criterion 1 requires for a within-person design. The starting condition was assigned at random, everyone switched for the second task, and the Limitations say 'roles were counterbalanced'. Unit within_person_order and structure crossover are valid codes in form-spec.md and fit this design.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.1; p. 14, Section 5.5; form-spec.md (assignment.unit, assignment.structure)

confirmed.statement: What was assigned is access to ChatGPT for the student's own ideation. AI-assisted students worked in a computer lab with 'limited internet access to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5)' and wrote and drew their own eight ideas on paper sheets. No condition differs only in whose output is evaluated.

The tool is generative AI. The abstract names 'generative AI, specifically ChatGPT', and the lab gave access to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), a chatbot built on a large language model. Role open_chat fits: the paper describes no usage instructions, studies 'the spontaneous integration of AI into creative workflows', and codes the students' own prompts.
confirmed.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Section 2 (question 4); p. 5, Section 3.2.1; p. 12, Tables 8 and 9

confirmed.statement: The comparison arm matches the form (ai = none, so ai_vs_bau). Unaided students sat in a classroom 'without computer access or permission to use any external resources or electronic devices'.
Task order was fixed for everyone (T1 public transport, then T2 university spaces), as what_was_assigned says. The random order therefore also decides which task a student does with ChatGPT.

The arm entries match Fig. 1 and the text. AI-assisted: Group B in T1 (27 students, 195 ideas) and Group A in T2 (24 students, 173 ideas), 368 ideas. Unaided: Group A in T1 (24, 158) and Group B in T2 (27, 202), 360 ideas. n = 51 per condition. Per-arm n_randomized = null is right for a crossover.

confirmed.statement: The ai_tool.how_used numbers match the PDF: 49 of 51 conversations retrieved, 341 units of analysis, 6.96 prompts per conversation, and Generic Idea Generation 165 (48.39 percent). The deliverable was handwritten, so AI text was not pasted in.

confirmed.statement: preregistered = not_stated is right. A search of the full text finds no preregistration, registry, or ethics-approval statement.

Caveats, no code change. The paper does not say how the random division was made. The two conditions also differ in room and computer access (computer lab vs classroom). The Task 2 unaided arm (Group B) had used ChatGPT in Task 1, which the paper flags as a possible carryover; the form records this in the Task 2 control-arm labels and in notes.

summary: The PDF supports each part of the assignment coding for S1: the 51 students were randomly divided into two groups that did one ideation task with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and one with no aid, in opposite orders, so the order of conditions was randomized (pp. 1, 4-5, 8, 14; Fig. 1). Access to ChatGPT for the students' own handwritten ideas is what was assigned, the comparison arm had no computer or external resources (ai = none), and the arm counts and ai_tool details match the PDF.
